taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Acceptable Use Policies Protect Platforms from Liability, Not People from Harm
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description:
A Belief within accelerationist discourse that platform-level enforcement mechanisms such as cloud provider acceptable use policies, app store review processes, and cyber insurance underwriting protect the platform or deploying company but provide no remedy channel for individuals harmed by AI systems deployed on those platforms.
Encompasses: the absence of third-party beneficiary standing under platform contracts, the inability of platform ToS enforcement to detect emergent algorithmic discrimination, the structural orientation of cyber insurance toward company financial exposure rather than victim compensation.
Excludes: the claim that platform gatekeepers provide zero useful governance, the sufficiency of private right of action alone without complementary detection mechanisms.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: The speaker extends the belief beyond platform AUPs to financial infrastructure (payment processors, app stores, cloud compute). The turn provides specificity (NCMEC reporting model, delisting triggers, AUP transparency reports) that narrows the belief's scope: it is not that all platform governance is liability-protective, but specifically that content-centric and AUP-based governance cannot reach the commercial revenue streams that sustain abuse ecosystems.

arguments.argument: The most effective near-term intervention may be targeting the financial infrastructure — payment processors, app stores, advertising networks, and cloud compute providers — that sustains the nonconsensual deepfake ecosystem, rather than focusing primarily on model developers or hosting platforms. The CSAM enforcement model's greatest successes came not from criminalizing camera manufacturers or even hosting platforms alone, but from choking financial flows: Visa, Mastercard, and PayPal cutting off payment processing to sites hosting CSAM materially reduced the commercial viability of those sites. The same chokepoint strategy applied to deepfake pornography services — requiring payment processors to refuse transactions with identified NCII-generating services, requiring app stores to delist face-swap apps that lack provenance embedding, and requiring cloud providers to include acceptable-use terms enforceable via compute-access revocation — would impose costs at bottlenecks that are far fewer in number, far more jurisdictionally reachable, and far harder to route around than either model weights or individual hosting platforms.
arguments.why_missing: The Skeptic focuses on platform and developer accountability as the upstream fix. The Safetyist is invested in the pharmaceutical pre-deployment evaluation analogy and layered supply-chain obligations centered on model developers. The Accelerationist focuses on criminal law and platform-side transparency mandates. None of them center the financial and infrastructure intermediaries as the primary enforcement lever, because each perspective is locked into a debate about where in the model-to-platform pipeline the obligation should sit — overlooking that the most practically enforceable chokepoints may lie outside that pipeline entirely, in the payment and distribution infrastructure that makes the abuse commercially viable. The CSAM financial-chokepoint precedent is mentioned in passing by the Accelerationist but never developed into a primary policy proposal.

arguments.argument: All three debaters implicitly assume that the primary policy problem is the creation and distribution of deepfake images, but the most acute and least-addressed harm vector is the weaponization of the mere threat of creating such images — deepfake-enabled coercion, extortion, and intimate partner abuse where no image need ever be publicly distributed. A victim who is told 'I can generate explicit images of you and send them to your employer' suffers coercive control regardless of whether the image is ever made. Existing revenge porn statutes, platform takedown obligations, and provenance watermarking are all irrelevant to this threat-based harm because there is no content to detect, no platform to hold liable, and no watermark to trace. Addressing this requires criminal statutes specifically targeting deepfake-enabled threats and coercion as a distinct offense category, funded victim support services, and public education campaigns — none of which appear in any debater's framework.
arguments.why_missing: Every debater has structured their argument around a content-centric model of harm: an image is created, distributed, and must be detected and removed. The Skeptic focuses on takedown burdens and platform accountability for hosted content. The Accelerationist focuses on criminal liability for creation and distribution plus platform transparency. The Safetyist focuses on pre-deployment evaluation and provenance to trace generated content. None of them address the scenario where the harm is entirely in the credible threat enabled by the technology's existence, because their shared framing treats the image itself as the locus of harm rather than the power asymmetry the technology creates. This is a genuine blind spot: the coercion use case is well-documented in intimate partner violence research but falls outside the content-moderation paradigm all three perspectives operate within.
